applicabilityConditions.analysis: temporal averaging: 2 frames for tactile trials, 8 frames for injection trials, to reduce noise; motion correction by SIFT-based registration; brain masking by flood fill (scikit-image flood); bleach correction: subtract the bottom 5% of pixels within the brain from each frame; baseline autofluorescence subtraction
applicabilityConditions.anesthesia: 3-4% isoflurane for induction; maintained at 1.25-1.5% during imaging (from trial file names); depth confirmed by loss of righting reflex, ~1 breath per second, no toe-pinch response
applicabilityConditions.imaging: 10 frames per second, 13.4 x 11.3 mm, 5 um/px with no binning; cropped to the brain and binned 4 x 4 for all trials
applicabilityConditions.invasiveness: through-skull, label-free; no craniotomy, no transgenic animals, no dye or virus injection
applicabilityConditions.preparation: head-fixed with earbars in a stereotaxic frame (Kopf); heating pad; hair removed with Nair; eye ointment; 1 mL body-temperature sterile saline subcutaneous; 0.1 mL 1% lidocaine subcutaneous under the scalp; scalp removed; periosteum cleaned; thin layer of cyanoacrylate glue applied to the skull for optical clarity
applicabilityConditions.readout: flavoprotein autofluorescence, dF/F over a region of interest
applicabilityConditions.statistics: none reported; no significance testing, no power analysis, no detection limit stated anywhere in the pub

confidence.basis: one mouse per trial, five mice in total, no statistics, no detection limit and no blinding reported; the pub is framed as a demonstration rather than a powered study

cost.note: 13 imaging trials across 5 mice. The pub reports the imaging system cost (approximately US$30,000 including the camera) as capital, not as the cost of this study; no per-study cost is given.

hypothesis: Determine whether in vivo flavoprotein autofluorescence imaging can measure brain responses to touch, capsaicin-induced pain and histamine-induced itch, as a behaviour-independent alternative to mouse behavioural assays.
invalidators: a repeat of the itch experiment with a sensitive genetically encoded calcium indicator that resolves a histamine-specific signal
the same experiment in non-anaesthetized animals, since anaesthesia suppresses cortical activity
an injection-artifact control that separates needle and handling responses from the pruritogen response
nextSteps: Repeat the itch experiments with a sensitive genetically encoded calcium indicator such as GCaMP to increase signal, testing the hypothesis that too few itch-responsive neurons produce too little autofluorescence to detect above noise.
Perform the experiments on non-anesthetized animals, because anesthesia is known to suppress cortical activity (ref 33).

Repeat the capsaicin experiments to distinguish activity patterns inherent to the brain from those caused by experimental variability, and determine what injection location, dose and prior-injection factors contribute to the oscillations.
Test analgesic drugs to see whether they alleviate pain-related sensory activity in the brain, as a check on drug-screening applicability.
Perform this imaging on chronic mouse pain and itch models rather than the acute models used here.
openQuestions: Why did we see no reproducible activity in response to itch?
How could we improve the methodology to enable this measurement?
outcomeSummary: Touch produced localized contralateral somatosensory signals and capsaicin produced widespread oscillatory cortical activation absent in vehicle trials; histamine produced activation indistinguishable from saline and inconsistent between trials, so the itch application was iced.

provenanceNotes: Icebox statement: Our original goal was to employ this technique to complement traditional mouse behavioral assays for itch. Using widefield autofluorescence microscopy, we observed no consistent brain activity in response to histamine-induced itch. We're therefore icing this concept for now.

Mouse identity per trial is not given in the pub. Trials are grouped into animals here from the authors' 'same mouse as in B/C' statements and shared session dates; those groupings are inferred, not stated.
The pub says vehicle trials were imaged for 10 minutes, while the figure legends and the deposited file names say 15 minutes. The trial table follows the file names.
Figure 3D is described as the same mouse as Figure 3C, but its Data IDs carry an earlier session date (2024-03-18) than 3C (2024-03-19). Recorded as printed.
No statistical test, power analysis or detection limit appears anywhere in the pub; effect values are therefore qualitative or single-trial.
question: Can label-free, through-skull flavoprotein autofluorescence imaging of the mouse cortex measure brain responses to touch, capsaicin-induced pain and histamine-induced itch, as an alternative to mouse behavioural assays?

successCriteria: A localized, reproducible cortical signal for each of the three stimuli, distinguishable from its vehicle or unstimulated control, in anaesthetized mice.
title: Label-free flavoprotein imaging of the mouse cortex as a behaviour-independent assay for touch, pain and itch (iced)
